name: Mediterranean diet
lead: The Mediterranean diet is a traditional eating pattern of countries such as Greece, southern Italy and Spain. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and extra-virgin olive oil, with moderate fish, poultry, eggs and dairy, low to moderate wine with meals, and limited red meat and sweets.[12] Researcher Ancel Keys popularised the idea after the Seven Countries Study.[12]

It is among the best-studied dietary patterns. Large cohort and trial evidence, including the PREDIMED trial in Spain and the Lyon Diet Heart Study, examined cardiovascular outcomes, and a Greek cohort linked adherence to survival.[1][2][3][4] Appearance communities cite it as an evidence-based alternative to fad diets for skin and general health; direct trials on skin or looks were not identified.
infobox: Olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish, nuts

paras: Core features include abundant plant foods, olive oil as the main fat, fish two to three times a week, and limited red meat; the pattern is often shown as a pyramid with physical activity and shared meals at its base.[5][12] A 1995 paper described the Mediterranean diet pyramid as a cultural model for healthy eating.[5]

Early studies in the 1950s and 1960s in southern Italy and Crete contributed data; the Seven Countries Study was directed by Ancel Keys and published in 1970, and the Keys' publicized the diet from 1975.[12] UNESCO recognised the Mediterranean diet as intangible cultural heritage in 2010.[12]

The Lyon Diet Heart Study, a randomized secondary prevention trial, reported lower recurrence of cardiac events after myocardial infarction in people eating a Mediterranean-type diet, and an earlier trial examined an alpha-linolenic acid-rich Mediterranean diet in coronary heart disease.[4][10]

The PREDIMED trial in Spain randomized people at high cardiovascular risk to Mediterranean diets supplemented with olive oil or nuts, or to a control diet, and reported fewer major cardiovascular events in the Mediterranean groups, in 2013 and in a 2018 republished analysis.[2][3] A Greek cohort of 22,043 adults linked adherence to greater survival.[1] A trial compared weight loss with low-carbohydrate, Mediterranean and low-fat diets.[6] A study reported that high adherence changes gut microbiota and metabolome.[8] A 2019 Cochrane review is described by Wikipedia as finding modest cardiovascular benefits with low-to-moderate certainty.[12] No clinical studies on skin or facial appearance were found.
Grokipedia notes that confounding by lifestyle, cost of olive oil and nuts, and varying definitions limit generalisation outside Mediterranean countries; this is AI-generated and unverified.[11]

card.summary: The best-researched diet pattern: strong cardiovascular data, but nothing on looks directly.
card.note: Appearance benefits are inferred from general health data.

quick.overview:
The Mediterranean diet is a plant-forward pattern built on olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish and nuts. It is widely studied.

Trials and cohorts address cardiovascular outcomes and survival; skin and appearance outcomes have not been directly tested.
quick.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms include unsaturated fats, fibre and polyphenols, and effects on gut microbiota; this is explanatory rather than proven for looks.
quick.risks: Cost and nutrient gaps outside original cultural settings have been noted; moderate wine is part of the traditional pattern.
